strengths: Resolves an important open question from Balcan et al. (2025) by extending multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning guarantees from 1D to p-dimensional case
Novel technical approach combining first-order logic and quantifier elimination from real algebraic geometry with learning theory, creating an interesting new connection
Removes restrictive assumptions (ELICQ conditions) from prior work and handles the more realistic bi-level validation setting (f ≠ g)
Theorem 4.1 improves upon Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) by removing dependence on data dimension q and an extra factor of p in the bound
Comprehensive framework providing analysis at multiple levels: general bounds, refined bounds with explicit solution paths, and applications beyond piecewise polynomial assumptions
Clear presentation with good motivation and well-organized structure making the problem and approach accessible
weaknesses: Completely absent empirical validation: no experiments, sample complexity measurements, or practical algorithm implementations demonstrating whether bounds are meaningful
Bounds are very loose and dimension-dependent: Theorem 5.1 has O(pd log(...) + p²d log(...)), Theorem 6.1 has O(pd² log(...) + p²d² log(...)), becoming impractical for moderate dimensions
Missing lower bounds for the general bi-level case: only upper bounds provided, leaving unclear whether they are fundamental or analysis artifacts. Only specific cases achieve tight bounds

Restrictive structural assumptions persist: requires piecewise polynomial structure excluding common ML objectives (exp, log, sigmoid), and Assumption 7.1 requires explicit solution paths that may not exist

Limited technical novelty: primary contribution (Theorem 4.1) combines existing results (Basu et al. 2006 quantifier elimination and Bartlett et al. 2022 GJ framework); Theorems 5.1-6.1 are straightforward applications
Quantifier elimination bounds are known to be loose in practice, yet paper doesn't discuss this limitation or provide tighter analysis for the specific settings studied
Complete absence of practical validation or guidance: no discussion of determining structural parameters for real problems, no comparison with practical methods, no computational complexity analysis

strengths: Resolves important open question: Successfully extends multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning framework from 1D to p-dimensional case
Novel model-theoretic approach: Elegant connection between FOL definability and pseudo-dimension with improved bounds over Goldberg-Jerrum (removes q-dependence and factors p)
Comprehensive theoretical treatment: Provides upper bounds (Theorems 5.1, 6.1), first general lower bound (Theorem 5.2), and refined bounds via solution paths (Theorem 7.2)
Removes restrictive assumptions: Eliminates ELICQ conditions, handles bi-level validation setting (f ≠ g), extends to semi-algebraic functions, and handles approximate optimization
Well-written and clear: Good motivation, effective examples (ridge regression), accessible treatment of FOL and quantifier elimination concepts
Demonstrates framework generality: Applications to weighted group LASSO and fused LASSO show versatility beyond piecewise polynomial assumptions
weaknesses: No practical validation: Purely theoretical with no algorithms, empirical evaluation, or evidence that bounds are tight; large gap between theory and practice
Potentially loose sample complexity bounds: O(pd²log M) terms with products in exponent; for large d or K, bounds could be prohibitively large with no tightness analysis
Incomplete lower bounds: Missing lower bound for main bi-level validation setting (Theorem 6.1); only training loss (Theorem 5.2) has lower bound
Limited tightness characterization: Only one complete matching upper-lower result (elastic net in Appendix F.2); unclear when theoretical bounds are tight in practice
Restrictive structural assumptions: Piecewise polynomial assumption still quite restrictive; cannot handle transcendental functions (exp, log, tanh), limiting applicability to neural networks
Somewhat incremental technical approach: Heavy reliance on Basu et al. (2006) quantifier elimination as black-box and existing Goldberg-Jerrum framework; main novelty is in problem formulation
Section 7 results are narrow: Theorem 7.2 requires strong Assumption 7.1 (explicit solution path); only two applications shown satisfying it
Limited algorithmic insights: Paper is purely complexity-theoretic with no guidance on computational complexity of quantifier elimination or practical algorithm design
Heavy appendix burden: Proofs relegated to appendix (A-G) makes complete verification difficult and suggests main text presentation could be improved
